12171-women-workers-in-seven-professions:
Edith J. Morley edited this 1914 survey for the Fabian Women Group Studies Committee, gathering first-hand essays on women work in seven professions. The writers speak from inside their trades, and Morley admits the book lacks unity by design.

Essays cover teaching, medicine, nursing, the civil service, and other fields open to educated women, with facts on pay, hours, promotion, and marriage bars. The evidence shows talent blocked by custom and low wages, and the writers argue for training, organization, and equal entry. As a document, the survey captures professional women on the eve of war, measuring progress and naming the barriers that remained.
13035-the-goop-directory-of-juvenile-off:
Gelett Burgess's 1913 Goop Directory lists naughty children in verse, each with a crime and a picture. Its index runs from Marmaduke Argyll, talking while eating, to Nancy Beal, throwing things away, and Betsy Birch, talking in church. Every Goop is a warning, dressed as a joke.

Verses scold Levi Boing for bumping into chairs, Mary C. C. Call for crying without end, and Miss Mackadoo for never answering when spoken to. The moral is plain: good children do the opposite of Goops. Short, rhymed, and meant to be read aloud, the book is a comic conduct guide from an age that taught manners by teasing.
1488-the-true-story-of-christopher-colum:
Elbridge S. Brooks's True Story of Christopher Columbus was written for the four-hundredth anniversary of 1492 and the Chicago Columbian Exposition. It follows Columbus from a boy with an idea to the admiral of the ocean sea. Chapters trace what people thought of his plan, his struggle for ships, and the great voyage itself.

Written for young readers, the book tells the voyages, the landfalls, and the later troubles in a plain, admiring style. Modern readers will note its hero-worship and its limits. It remains a period piece of American history writing for children, and a window on how 1892 honoured Columbus.
17548-letters-concerning-poetical-transl:
Printed in London in 1739 for J. Roberts near the Oxford Arms in Warwick Lane, and sold for one shilling, this small book gathers letters on poetical translation and on the arts of verse of Virgil and Milton. The first letter opens with an apology for writing in the author's own way, as much or as little at a time as inclination allows, and just as things offer themselves.

Readers get an early eighteenth-century discussion of how to carry poetry from one tongue to another, and of what makes Virgil's and Milton's verse work. The letters are informal, learned, and opinionated, in the manner of Augustan criticism. They suit students of translation, of Milton, and of the literary talk of 1739.
21476-salt-water-the-sea-life-and-advent:
Neil D'Arcy goes to sea as a midshipman under his uncle's care in W. H. G. Kingston's Salt Water. Kingston wrote the book early, and no new edition appeared for sixty years. Blows and buffetings await Neil, as he owns at the start, but they never change his wishes.

Most of the action lies in the Mediterranean, out to the Ionian Sea. Neil visits Zante, Cephalonia, and Corfu between fights and sudden deaths. Nearly every other figure in the tale is slain before the end. Neil alone survives all, in a rattling yarn of battle and chance.
22228-alphabetical-vocabularies-of-the-c:
George Gibbs, a lawyer and ethnologist on the Pacific coast, compiled these vocabularies of the Clallam and Lummi languages. The Smithsonian Institution published them in 1863 in Shea's Library of American Linguistics. Gibbs had lived among the peoples of Puget Sound and the Strait of Georgia. His word lists record languages then spoken daily from Cape Flattery to Vancouver Island.

Each vocabulary runs alphabetically, English headword first, then the Native word. Gibbs notes kinships with the Chemakum, Songish, and Sooke dialects nearby. Such lists were salvage work, made as settlement broke up Native life. Linguists still use them: for some words, Gibbs is the earliest or only written witness.
27231-the-riflemen-of-the-miami:
Edward S. Ellis's The Riflemen of the Miami, published by Beadle in 1862, opens with a rescue on the Miami River. Four men move under the bank, bodies bent, rifles and hunting-knives in hand, peering over the bank at something in the open wood.

Two are brothers, George and Lewis Dernor, the third answers to Dick, real name Richard Allmat, and a fourth brings up the rear. Ellis writes a dime-novel frontier tale of woodmen on civilization's confines, quick, careful, and ready with the Macbeth motto: if it were done, then it were well done quickly.
28180-hanover-or-the-persecution-of-the-:
Jack Thorne wrote Hanover, or The Persecution of the Lowly, as a story of the Wilmington massacre of 1898. Thorne dedicates the book to Ida B. Wells Barnett, the anti-lynching heroine, and opens with press reports of Black citizens fleeing Wilmington, driven out by organized Red Shirts. Three hundred white men were sworn in as police, and trade stood still.

The novel follows lowly Black and white citizens ordered out of town, as a mayor and his police halt further killing yet leave white rule in place. Thorne writes with partisan heat for the victims. The book stands as an early, rare fictional record of a violent coup against a biracial government.
3115-the-indeterminate-sentence-what-sha:
Warner asks what should be done with the criminal class. Present methods, he says, were never tried on a fully scientific basis. The problem is at bottom economic and educational. It must rest on the principles that govern a sound industry or a school. Both the safety of society and the interests of the criminal deserve weight. Public indifference explains why so little progress has been made.

His proposal is the indeterminate sentence: punishment fitted to the person, not fixed in advance by a rigid term. The essay argues reform over revenge. It still frames prison debate today, on safety, fairness, and whether confinement should aim to change the offender.
31267-taxonomy-of-the-chipmunks-eutamias:
John A. White's 1953 paper, volume 5, number 33 of the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History series, sorts out two chipmunks, Eutamias quadrivittatus and Eutamias umbrinus. Chipmunk species differ only subtly in anatomy and color, White explains, so taxonomists need a chipmunk scale rather than a pocket-gopher scale, where allied forms differ markedly in size and skeleton.

The historical summary traces Merriam's 1905 separation of quadrivittatus, Howell's 1929 list of subspecies, Hardy's 1945 and Kelson's 1951 placements, and Johnson's 1943 restoration of speciosus. With six text figures, the paper is a careful revision of a group where close looking, not broad strokes, decides what counts as a species.
31730-subspeciation-in-the-meadow-mouse-:
Sydney Anderson's 1954 paper for the University of Kansas Museum of Natural History studies subspeciation in the meadow mouse, Microtus montanus, in Wyoming and Colorado. The species reaches the eastern limits of its range in those states, where it occupies the mountains but in general not the lowlands.

Anderson links the mouse's range to moisture, since the grasses it uses for food, protection from enemies, and shelter from the elements depend on it. Readers get a concise taxonomic study, mapping how one widespread mouse divides into local forms across mountain country.
3423-the-strolling-saint-being-the-confe:
Rafael Sabatini writes this novel as the confessions of a man torn between the cloister and the world. The hero begins as an oblate in Piacenza, raised among monks, and the first book follows his boyhood, his rebellion, and a figure called Fra Gervasio. Later books take him to the house of Astorre Fifanti, to a captain of justice, and at last to a hermit's life on Monte Orsaro.

The title's strolling saint is a man who cannot settle in either holiness or sin. Sabatini fills the journey with love, violence, and religious doubt, set in Renaissance Italy. Readers who enjoy historical romance with a moral edge will find a hero who questions his own motives at every turn.
66028-trial-of-the-major-war-criminals-b:
An official text in the English tongue fills this book, printed at Nuremberg in 1947. It holds the record of the trial of the major war criminals in front of the court of arms of the allied lands. That trial ran from 14 November 1945 to 1 October 1946. The book came out by the word of the court itself, through its own staff, under the rule of the Allied Control Authority for Germany.

This is the twelfth book of the set. It holds the days of the trial from 18 April 1946 to 2 May 1946. The list of parts names each day and its parts: the time of dawn and the time past noon. The 111th day starts the book, a Thursday, and the count runs through the 116th day.
britannica-1911-agoranomi:
Agoranomi were magistrates in the republics of Greece. Their duties resembled those of Rome's aediles. Market order was their central charge in Athens. Ten of them were chosen annually by lot. Five took charge of the city itself. Five took charge of the Peiraeus, the port. They settled disputes arising in the markets. They examined the quality of goods exposed for sale.

Weights and measures fell under their testing. Agoranomi checked both for honesty in trade. They collected the harbour dues for the state. Shipping regulations were theirs to enforce as well. The entry gives a complete job description briefly. Lot, not election, filled these offices yearly. Athens split the board evenly between city and port.
britannica-1911-bagirmi:
Bagirmi is a country of north-central Africa, south-east of Lake Chad. It forms part of the Chad district of French Congo. It runs 240 miles north to south. Its 20,000 square miles are near-flat clay land. Its 1903 population was put at 100,000, much thinned by wars and slave raiding.

The Shari river bounds it west, and its tributaries cross the country, though swamps and sand-choked channels swallow much water and droughts return often. The south is most fertile; millet and sesame lead the crops, cotton and indigo grow too, and elephants, hippos, and lions range the wilds. The capital is Chekna, the older capital Massenia having been destroyed in 1898. Trade runs to Yola, to Khartum through Wadai, and by an old caravan road across the Sahara to Tripoli.
britannica-1911-boue-ami:
Ami Boué (1794–1881) was an Austrian geologist born at Hamburg who helped found organised geology in France. Schooled at Hamburg, Geneva, and Paris, he went to Edinburgh to study medicine and fell under Robert Jameson's teaching in geology and mineralogy. Field trips across Scotland and the Hebrides set his course.

He took his medical degree in 1817, settled in Paris, and in 1820 issued his Essai géologique sur l'Écosse, with careful accounts of the eruptive rocks. Travels across Germany, Austria, and southern Europe made him a pioneer of the science. In 1830 he was a founder of the Société Géologique de France and its president in 1835. Settled at Vienna from 1841 as a naturalised Austrian, he sent the Vienna academy major papers on the geology of the Balkan states.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-chicoutimi:
Created in May 1878, the Diocese of Chicoutimi covers Charlevoix, Chicoutimi, and Lac Saint-Jean in north-eastern Quebec. French settlers reached Charlevoix in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, while Chicoutimi and Lac Saint-Jean grew in the mid-nineteenth century from settlers of the Saint Lawrence valley. The mountain region holds the Saguenay River and the great lakes Saint-Jean and Mistassini, and its lumber trade has given way to farming and paper pulp.

Jesuits served the region until the end of the eighteenth century, Oblates until the mid-nineteenth, and secular priests since, and a small Jesuit church of 1747 still stands at Tadousac. Parishes grew from 24 in 1878 to 55 in 1907, served by 105 secular and 18 regular priests for about 66,000 people. Marist Brothers run six colleges, sisters of many orders staff hospitals, orphanages, and convents, and 15,000 children attend 310 parish schools.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-caris:
Giacomo Carissimi was the most influential and prolific Italian composer of his day, born at Marino in 1604 and dead at Rome in 1674. After training in Rome he led the choir at Assisi, then from 1628 at St. Apollinaris in Rome. A Catholic Encyclopedia article credits him as the father of the modern oratorio, the sacred musical drama later perfected by Handel and Bach.

He shaped the form from the simple sacred songs written for St. Philip Neri's prayer meetings. He gave the recitative a lyric quality, varied the orchestral accompaniment, and drove the whole forward with drama. Many of his oratorios are lost, but manuscripts survive in Paris, Oxford, and Rome. His pupils included Alessandro Scarlatti and Marc-Antoine Charpentier, carrying his manner into the next generation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-ingh:
Giovanni Inghirami was an Italian astronomer born at Volterra in 1779, who died at Florence in 1851. Of a noble family, he joined the Piarists at seventeen and later taught mathematics and philosophy at Volterra, where the future Pius IX was among his pupils. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a scientist of simplicity and piety who worked almost blind to the end.

Called to Florence, he taught mathematics and astronomy at San Giovannino and directed its observatory. After fourteen years of observation he published, in 1830, a topographic and geometric map of Tuscany. Drawn on a scale of one to two hundred thousand, it was a work of high merit. He also won praise for his section of the Berlin Academy's star atlas. He served as provincial and general of his order before resigning for his health.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-joseph-anthel:
Joseph Anthelmi was a French priest and church historian who lived from 1648 to 1697. Born at Fréjus, he studied theology at Lyons under Père Lachaise, later confessor to Louis XIV. Ordained and made a canon of Fréjus Cathedral, he devoted himself to Provence's church history.

Anthelmi is best known for two learned disputes. Against Pasquier Quesnel he defended St. Prosper of Aquitaine as author of works Quesnel gave to St. Leo the Great. He also argued that the Athanasian Creed came not from Athanasius but from a fifth-century Gaul, likely St. Vincent of Lérins. Readers find a portrait of a sharp, local scholar in national debate.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-minimi:
The Minimi, or Minims, are the religious order founded by St. Francis of Paula. The name alludes to Friar Minor, or to Matthew 25:40, whatever you did for one of the least of my brethren, you did for me. As Leo X said in the founder's canonization bull, it suggests the great humility that should mark the order, whose members ought to count themselves least of all religious. A second order for sisters and a third order for seculars are connected with the first.

St. Francis of Paula was called to France in 1482, where the earliest convents stood at Plessis-les-Tours, Amboise, and Nigeon near Paris. The French Minims, famed for simplicity, were called bons hommes. Their distinctive fourth vow, vita quadragesimalis, imposes perpetual abstinence from flesh meat. Since the French Revolution the order has shrunk to nineteen convents and about 330 friars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salimbene-deg:
Salimbene degli Adami, also called Ognibene, was a Franciscan chronicler born at Parma on 9 October 1221 who died probably at Montefalcone about 1288. From a distinguished family, he entered the order about 1238 despite his father's violent efforts to drag him back. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia introduces one of the liveliest witnesses of thirteenth-century Italy.

Wandering between houses at Florence, Parma, Ravenna, Reggio, and Montefalcone, he met scholars of his day, Pope Innocent IV, and Emperor Frederick II. Near the end of his life he wrote a chronicle covering 1167 to 1287, first printed in part at Parma in 1857, with its opening section edited by Clédat in 1878. Gossipy, sharp-eyed, and often partisan, it remains a first-rate source for Franciscan life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tomi:
Tomi was a titular metropolitan see in Scythia, on the Black Sea, founded as a Greek colony from Miletus. Rome took the country from the Odrysae in 29 BC, annexing it as far as the Danube, and from Diocletian's time Tomi served as metropolis of Scythia Minor. In AD 10 Augustus exiled Ovid there, and the poet died there eight years later, singing the town's praises in his verse.

Few towns hold so many Christian memories, in what the entry calls the barbarous country of the Getae. Martyrs Macrobius and Gordianus died in exile in 319, Argeus, Narcissus and Marcellinus under Licinius, and many others fill the martyrology for April, June, July and October. Its bishops include Bretanion under Valens, Theotimus, friend of Chrysostom, and John, a church writer who died about 448.
doe-osti-17019155-abbreviated-final-repo:
William Farmer of Lawrence Livermore wrote this abbreviated final report, dated September 2026, on atomic physics data for fusion modeling. Predictive simulation of inertial confinement fusion needs accurate data for highly charged gold ions in hot plasma. Older calculations overpredicted x-ray emission and electron impact excitation for key gold transitions in the 2 to 4 keV range.

New calculations used two advanced methods to study nickel like, copper like, and zinc like gold ions. Correlation effects proved modest for the nickel like case but much stronger for the other two, where inner shells mix heavily. Adding those effects lowered selected rates and cross sections, bringing results closer to electron beam ion trap measurements.
doe-osti-2997291-progress-towards-a-full:
Kenneth Cundiff, Kevin Long, and James Hartley wrote Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2025-12286R, dated 26 September 2025. The report builds a math model for how semicrystalline polymers swell and shrink as they crystallize and melt. The target material is the encapsulant plastic in solar panels, which can partly crystallize during service outdoors. Volume change inside a sealed panel stresses the cells it protects.

Each material point blends two phases under one energy law: a crystalline part treated as simple elastic solid, and an amorphous part treated as a slow-flowing viscoelastic solid. The crystalline share evolves with temperature and rate, and a mixing heat term produces the volume strain. The model joins Sandia's materials library and ships in the next Sierra solid mechanics release, version 5.26. Panel designers can now predict a strain they once had to guess.
doe-osti-2999993-ligated-cluster-buildin:
Arthur Reber of Virginia Commonwealth University wrote this final report for Energy Department award DE-SC0006420, covering July 2020 to June 2025. His group studies superatoms: small clusters of atoms, dressed with protective ligand shells, that behave like single super-sized atoms. Such clusters can donate or accept electrons on demand, making them building blocks for two-dimensional materials such as metal chalcogenide sheets and phosphorene ribbons only atoms thick.

The report counts 31 papers published or submitted since 2020, with 14 crediting this grant, plus a co-edited book on metal clusters. Highlights include stable clusters beyond the usual magic numbers, magnetic superatoms that drew wide press attention, and transport work featured on a journal cover. Reber chaired the first session of a new Gordon conference on atomically precise nanochemistry in 2024. One master's and two doctoral theses came from the group. The record closes with publications, talks and collaborations.
doe-osti-3001524-probing-ultrafast-charg:
Joshua Vura-Weis of the University of Illinois files the final report for award DE-SC0021062 on the first instants after sunlight hits a solar material. Quantum dot solar cells pair light absorbing dots with metal oxides. Efficiency past the single junction limit may hide in hot electrons and multiple excitons, charge carriers squeezed from one photon. But charge can trap and recombine uselessly, and the steps are debated.

The programme watched those steps. Ultrafast X ray spectroscopies ran at synchrotrons and free electron lasers, in absorption, emission and scattering variants. They followed charge density and structure in lead and cadmium chalcogenide dots linked or grown onto oxides. X ray methods separate donor from acceptor behaviour in ways optical probes cannot. Results resolve the timescales of charge separation against the loss routes, for linked and epitaxial structures alike. The report is concise, a goals and findings summary.
doe-osti-3002207-as-run-neutronic-calcul:
Ariel Márquez gives analysts a how-to guide in Oak Ridge report ORNL/TM-2025/4110, dated October 2025. The guide covers as-run neutronic calculations for MiniFuel experiments in the High Flux Isotope Reactor. As-run means the calculation follows the test as it actually ran, not as planned. MiniFuel tests irradiate tiny fuel samples, and their neutron exposure must be reconstructed afterward.

Step by step, the guide sets out modeling choices, inputs, and checks that keep different analysts consistent. It points to the HFIRCON code manual and to earlier separate-effects test literature. Consistent as-run numbers let experimenters convert raw test results into burnup and flux values that models can use. The document is a reference for new analysts joining the MiniFuel program and for reviewers checking their work.
doe-osti-3005579-rolling-behavior-of-sur:
Cheryl Lynn Hawk, Lindsay Beth O'Brien, Nickolas James Gandara, and five colleagues test a tracking idea in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-31524, issued November 24, 2025. The idea is intentional tagging of nuclear fuel: mark material with photoluminescent oxides that glow under the right light. A tag that survives processing could identify lost or diverted fuel later, a goal of the intentional forensics program.

This study rolls tagged aluminum 6061, mimicking a fuel fabrication step, and watches how the taggant behaves. Rolling can bury, smear, or destroy a surface tag, so survival through it is a real test. The tag should also leave the metal's corrosion and strength behavior alone. Earlier Los Alamos work tagged the same alloy system; this report extends it through deformation. The work is dated September 2024 on its internal title page.
doe-osti-3008958-metal-encapsulation-str:
Yearly progress report for DOE award DE-SC0022197 covers three funded years on using less platinum-group metal in emission control catalysts. Matteo Cargnello of Stanford University submitted it on December 17, 2025, with co-investigators at SLAC, Stanford, and Oak Ridge. The strategy wraps metal nanoparticles in thin oxide shells so they cannot clump and die.

Trace amounts of alumina laid down by atomic layer deposition stopped platinum particles from sintering. The rhodium work delivered a warning instead: rhodium particles encapsulated after 50 deposition cycles performed worse after accelerated aging than plain supported ones. Ceria promoters and an expanding library of coatings and templates round out the program.
doe-osti-3013840-integrated-life-cycle-a:
West Virginia University's Jingxin Wang led this final report for award DE-FE0032212, submitted January 21, 2026, covering October 2022 to September 2025. Mandal, Kirumira, Grandhi, and co-authors assessed whether Central Appalachia's legacy mine lands could host biomass production while their waste coal gets used rather than left in piles. Both moves promise income for coal country and cleanup of scarred land.

The team paired life cycle assessment with techno-economic analysis, counting emissions and costs from site preparation through end use. Scenarios weighed growing energy crops on reclaimed mines against the expense of hauling and processing waste coal. The report gives developers and policymakers a region-specific evidence base rather than national averages, which matter where terrain and haul distances dominate the economics.
doe-osti-3015556-a-reproducible-study-de:
Predicting in-hospital deaths from intensive care records gets a reproducible study design in ORNL/TM-2026/4421, dated January 2026, by Stanley, Gounley, and Hanson at Oak Ridge National Laboratory. Studies on the MIMIC-IV database often cannot be repeated because preprocessing choices go undocumented, so the authors pin down the full pipeline.

Their design covers dataset construction, a documented preprocessing pipeline, feature selection with statistical screening, and custom clinical groupings, including non-chart features such as central lines, dialysis, and intubation that mark illness severity. On aggregated features the best model reached an AUC of 79.54 percent. Rebuilt as time series, logistic regression and XGBoost both improved, with XGBoost best at 80.69 percent AUC and a 79.34 percent macro F1 score, a result the authors credit to dynamic features capturing temporal patterns.
doe-osti-3018445-executive-summary-for-t:
Claudio S Montanari of Fermilab wrote this summary, FERMILAB-TM-2926-PPD, dated December 4, 2025. It covers a research program written for the DOE Genesis Mission. Three technical notes build a speculative but strict cosmology. In that framework, spacetime geometry emerges from a replication-driven break in a non-spatial domain. A one-to-many replication rule generates time order, spatial nearness, and a limiting causal speed. It also produces a two-layer vacuum, reheating, and a multi-peaked wave spectrum.

Much of the summary concerns method rather than cosmology. The framework was developed with OpenAI's ChatGPT 5.1 as a partner. The AI turned hunches into formal terms, built mid-step math, and checked global consistency across rounds. Montanari stresses that the system did not replace scientific judgment. His claim is narrower: AI can speed early theoretical work.
doe-osti-3020403-the-emergent-photophysi:
Joel Yuen-Zhou's final technical report for DOE Basic Energy Sciences award DE-SC0019188, from the University of California, San Diego, covers theory work on molecular polaritons from 2018 to 2025. When molecules sit between closely spaced mirrors, they merge with trapped light into hybrid states that are part matter, part photon. Experiments have shown these states can change the speed and outcome of some chemical reactions.

The puzzle is that the reactions happen in messy, lossy surroundings, with solvent molecules and mirrors that leak photons. Yuen-Zhou's group built quantum mechanical theories for how polaritons behave under those real conditions. Work with collaborators also extended the ideas to nanophotonic cavities, including plasmonic nanocrescents with unusual optical response. The report lays out a theoretical base for using light to steer chemistry.
doe-osti-3022673-from-cryogenic-to-high-:
Los Alamos National Laboratory report LA-UR-26-21857, by Alice Smith, follows the microstructure of delta-phase plutonium-gallium alloy from cryogenic cold to high temperature using time-of-flight neutron diffraction. The alloy studied carries 2 atomic percent gallium, which stabilizes the workable delta phase, and the measurements track lattice parameter and peak width through a full thermal cycle.

Samples were cooled from 298 kelvin to 10, then heated to 673 and returned to room temperature. Peak broadening introduced along the way needed heating above 550 kelvin to recover fully, and cooling back to 300 kelvin closed the hysteresis loop in peak width completely. The lattice parameter did not quite come home: it settled at 4.6252 plus or minus 0.0006 angstroms, 0.0017 angstroms larger than the as-heat-treated starting value.
doe-osti-3027392-multimodal-instrument-c:
Yaohua Liu of Oak Ridge National Laboratory sets out instrument concepts for chemical sciences at the Second Target Station in ORNL/TM-2026/4483, dated March 2026. The Second Target Station will expand the Spallation Neutron Source, and multimodal instruments would measure the same sample several ways at once. Chemistry users care about functional groups and how they transform during catalysis or thermal decomposition.

Vibrational spectroscopy earns a featured place for its feel for hydrogen. The proton's large incoherent scattering cross-section makes neutron vibrational spectra exceptionally sensitive to hydrogen motion, so proton dynamics and hydrogen vibrations show up even at very low concentrations. The full spectrum also yields the vibrational density of states, from which entropy and specific heat are derived, and small spectral shifts flag changes with temperature or environment.
doe-osti-3028606-coupled-hydrological-th:
David Fukuyama, Lisa Bigler, Olin Carty, and nine colleagues at Sandia National Laboratories present the CH4PACE project in SAND2025-12346R, printed September 2025. The name unpacks to coupled hydrological, thermal, and biogeochemical modeling for predicting Arctic carbon emissions. Thawing permafrost wakes microbes that release methane and carbon dioxide, and the size of that feedback is one of climate science's open numbers.

The team built models that move water, heat, and microbial chemistry together instead of in isolation. Parts of the report draw on manuscripts in preparation, including work on the effective permeability of permafrost submitted to Geophysical Research Letters and a University of Texas master's thesis by Riley Garrett. Funding came from Sandia's Earth science LDRD area and its Academic Alliance program, a detail the acknowledgements record.
doe-osti-3363548-probing-attosecond-boun:
Michael Chini files this final report on driving bound electron motion in atoms and molecules. The tools are near-single-cycle light pulses. The project built its sources on industrial grade ytterbium solid-state lasers. It aimed to rebuild time dependent wave packets from measurements. It also probed how those packets lose coherence, using attosecond timing. A further goal was steering dynamics on attosecond to few-femtosecond timescales.

The team compressed ytterbium laser pulses in gas filled hollow-core fibers. The effect used is called multidimensional solitary states. They built fast waveform measurement tools, both single-shot and real-time. They also made phase stable near-single-cycle pulses. With polarization gating, they showed phase dependent high-order harmonic generation. The award supported four doctoral dissertations.
doe-osti-3364900-bil-grid-ready-wind-rel:
General Electric's final technical report for DOE award DE-EE0010652 covers the BIL Grid-Ready Wind project at the Great Pathfinder Wind Power Plant, led by Reetam Sen Biswas with Rojan Bhattarai. The project, running October 2024 to October 2025, designed grid services that a wind plant can sell: grid-forming controls and ancillary services that steady a grid filling with inverter-based resources.

Progress was real but the demonstration stalled. The team drafted a white paper on grid stability challenges, briefed the ISO/RTO Council's emerging technologies group, and took feedback from SPP. Then demonstration partner APEX withdrew, and subcontracting delays compounded. Site-dependent tasks, test planning, and some hardware work wait on a replacement partner. The report is candid that the technology stays viable while the field trial does not yet exist.
doe-osti-3374702-total-effective-dose-fr:
INL/RPT-25-87815, an Idaho National Laboratory report, dated September 2025, by Kira B. Overin and A. Jeffrey Sondrup, computes the public dose from radioactive air emissions at lab facilities. The figures feed the population dose section of the lab's 2024 Annual Site Environmental Report. Such reports must show what dose nearby residents could receive from routine releases.

The work starts with a source term, the list of what each facility released. Air transport comes from HYSPLIT model runs over the site domain. A second code, DOSEMM, turns air and ground levels into total effective dose. Tables give dose factors element by element, from chlorine and cobalt to cesium and iodine. Decay and ingrowth of daughter products are built into the sums.
letters-concerning-poetical-translations:
William Benson published his Letters Concerning Poetical Translations in London in 1739. J. Roberts printed them near the Oxford Arms in Warwick Lane. Virgil's and Milton's arts of verse share his title.

Benson promises to write as much or little as inclination moves him. He compares Virgil's verse craft with Milton's across the letters. Translation raises hard questions about sense, sound, and freedom. Benson argues those questions through two epic masters. His letters show early English critics weighing classical and native poetry together. Benson had earlier edited Virgil's works with great labor. Milton's blank verse receives his special, careful praise.
nasa-tm-19680023902-experimental-investi:
Joseph F. Wasserbauer and Daniel L. Whipple of Lewis Research Center tested a supersonic inlet's dynamic response in this 1968 report. The inlet ran at Mach 3.0 in the 10-by-10-Foot Supersonic Wind Tunnel. Disturbances came from both outside and inside the inlet across wide frequency ranges.

The team measured terminal shock position and static pressure responses. For internal disturbances, the shock and throat pressure responses showed a lag pattern. That lag held up to a certain frequency in the tests described. Knowing this response helps designers keep inlets stable when conditions change suddenly. Unstable inlets can starve or damage the engines they feed.
nasa-tm-19680024853-microelectronic-data:
James H. Schrader and C. D. Nichols of Langley Research Center describe a microelectronic data system for wind tunnel testing in this June 1968 paper. Dynamic tests run long series of conditions with no practical access to the model. Engineers still need data out and control signals in throughout each run.

Their system sends up to twenty high-response data signals from the model. It also carries up to fifty-four auxiliary control functions back to the model. All traffic shares a single cable about one-sixteenth of an inch thick. Remote control covers the model's electromechanical transducers and full data system setup. The design suits dynamic transonic tunnel work, per the report record.
nasa-tm-19700023531-dissociation-rates-o:
Marvin Warshay of the Lewis Research Center wrote this report in July 1970. It measures how fast shock-heated bromine falls apart in the presence of helium and xenon. A shock wave can heat a gas so fast that its molecules break into atoms.

Warshay worked behind the moving shock in a shock tube. He tracked the bromine level by how much light the gas absorbed. The tests covered a wide span of high temperatures. He also gauged how well bromine itself works as a collision partner. Results of this kind feed the chemistry models used for very hot gas flows.
nasa-tm-19720002428-medical-information-:
S. Alterescu and colleagues described the Medical Information Management System, called MIMS, in this September 1971 report, NASA TM X-65747. MIMS was an automated hospital information system handling all data tied to patient care. The report was written for the people who would actually run it: nontechnical medical staff, not computer specialists.

The system is built from six program units, and the contents walk through them one by one. Units named Header, Store, and Retrieve handle setting up files, entering patient records, and pulling them back out. Worked examples show the system in daily operation, with commentary explaining each example. A complete listing of the system program is included, making the report a working manual as well as a description.
podcast-joerogan-ARaqe-0MKmI:
Writer and activist Maajid Nawaz sits for episode 1780 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Nawaz spent his youth in an Islamist group, left it, and built a career arguing for reform and free speech. His life story crosses several of the show's favorite themes at once.

He and Rogan talk about extremism, how minds get captured by movements, and the long road back out. Nawaz also speaks on censorship and the policing of speech in open societies. The episode gives listeners a rare first-hand guide to radical belief, from a man who held it, lost it, and now studies it.
the-goop-directory-of-juvenile-offenders: Gelett Burgess wrote The Goop Directory of Juvenile Offenders. He also wrote Goops. The book is dated 1913, with his own pictures. Its subtitle says the offenders serve as a salutary example. They serve for all virtuous children. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and an index of offenders. Each name is tagged with a fault. Marmaduke Argyll talks while eating. Nancy Beal throws away things. Master Bildad is selfish with toys. Amanda Fish steals sweets. Amelia Pratt says I won't. No verse text is present.
the-indeterminate-sentence-what-shall-be:
Charles Dudley Warner takes up the criminal class in this essay. He asks what the indeterminate sentence should do. Crime policy has never had a scientific trial, he argues. It must protect society. It must also serve the criminal's own interests. He calls the problem one of economics and schooling. Public apathy shares the blame for failure. Sentimental reformers share it too. They want deep reform without deep discipline.

Warner defines his subject with care. Not every lawbreaker belongs to the criminal class. The class lives by crime as a trade. Its members prey on society. The state itself trains most of them, he says. Short spells in lock-ups and jails school them. Each spell strips self-respect away. Escape from that machine is hard. His essay asks what should replace it.
the-strolling-saint-being-the-confession: Raphael Sabatini presents this historical novel as the confessions of the high and mighty Agostino D'Anguissola, tyrant of Mondolfo and lord of Carmina in the state of Piacenza. Only the title page and contents appear in this record. Two companion records carry the same front matter. Three books make up the novel. They are The Oblate, Giuliana, and The Wilderness. Their chapters cover Gino Falcone and Luisina. Rebellion, Fra Gervasio, and an iron girdle follow. The confessions themselves do not appear.
the-true-story-of-christopher-columbus-c:
Elbridge S. Brooks offers The True Story of Christopher Columbus, called the Great Admiral, as the opening volume of his Children's Lives of Great Men series. His preface inscribes the book to the boys and girls of America. Columbus takes the place of honour, Brooks says. Without his pluck, faith, and perseverance, young America might never have existed to read the book. His record of persistence through discouragement has inspired Americans ever since.

Chapter one, Boy with an Idea, begins simply: men who do great things are men we all like to read about, and Columbus lived four hundred years ago in Genoa. Brooks promises a straightforward, earnest telling in which the hero can be the man, and the man the hero. Written for the 400th anniversary of 1492, the book shows how its era taught children to revere the Admiral.
women-workers-in-seven-professions-a-sur:
Edith J. Morley edited this 1914 survey for the Studies Committee of the Fabian Women's Group. Her preface says the essays gather firsthand evidence. Each writer speaks from inside her own profession. Morley admits the pieces lack unity, yet she trusts real experience over polish. Women weighing a career were a main audience.

Sections cover fields such as medicine, nursing, teaching, and acting. Helpers named include Dr. Murrell and Mrs. Pember Reeves. The survey weighs pay, training, and prospects in each field. Readers get practical testimony about women's public work before the First World War.
